lessons.title: File permissions
lessons.summary: Unix mode bits grant read, write and execute rights separately to the owner, group and everyone else.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Unix mode bits grant read, write and execute rights separately to the owner, group and everyone else.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: For regular files, read exposes bytes, write changes bytes and execute permits execution. For directories, read lists names, execute traverses paths and write changes directory entries. Mode 640 grants owner read/write and group read; every parent directory still needs search permission.

lessons.takeaway: For regular files, read exposes bytes, write changes bytes and execute permits execution. For directories, read lists names, execute traverses paths and write changes directory entries. Mode 640 grants owner read/write and group read; every parent directory still needs search permission.

lessons.title: Ownership
lessons.summary: Each file has a numeric owner UID and group GID; names are lookups for those numbers.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Each file has a numeric owner UID and group GID; names are lookups for those numbers.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The kernel compares the process credentials with ownership and permission rules. chown changes ownership, while chmod changes mode bits. Supplementary groups and ACLs can affect access even when the displayed owner differs.

lessons.takeaway: The kernel compares the process credentials with ownership and permission rules. chown changes ownership, while chmod changes mode bits. Supplementary groups and ACLs can affect access even when the displayed owner differs.

lessons.title: Symbolic links
lessons.summary: A symbolic link is a filesystem object containing another pathname.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A symbolic link is a filesystem object containing another pathname.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The kernel follows the target during pathname resolution. Relative targets resolve from the link's directory, and targets can cross filesystems or disappear. Inspect the resolved path when a release link stops working.

lessons.takeaway: The kernel follows the target during pathname resolution. Relative targets resolve from the link's directory, and targets can cross filesystems or disappear. Inspect the resolved path when a release link stops working.

lessons.title: Hard links
lessons.summary: Hard links are multiple directory entries referring to the same inode on one filesystem.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Hard links are multiple directory entries referring to the same inode on one filesystem.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: They share content and metadata. Removing one name decreases the link count; storage is reclaimed only when no links or open references remain. A hard link is not a second independent backup.

lessons.takeaway: They share content and metadata. Removing one name decreases the link count; storage is reclaimed only when no links or open references remain. A hard link is not a second independent backup.

lessons.title: Pipelines
lessons.summary: A shell pipeline connects one program's standard output to another program's standard input.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A shell pipeline connects one program's standard output to another program's standard input.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The pipe buffers bytes and applies backpressure when the reader is slower. Standard error stays separate unless redirected. In Bash, pipefail makes a failing earlier stage affect pipeline status, which matters in automation.

lessons.takeaway: The pipe buffers bytes and applies backpressure when the reader is slower. Standard error stays separate unless redirected. In Bash, pipefail makes a failing earlier stage affect pipeline status, which matters in automation.

lessons.title: Quoting
lessons.summary: Shell quoting controls which expansions and special characters are interpreted by the shell.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Shell quoting controls which expansions and special characters are interpreted by the shell.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Double quotes allow variable expansion while preventing word splitting and globbing of the result. Single quotes preserve literal characters. Pass untrusted values as arguments rather than building shell code and evaluating it.

lessons.takeaway: Double quotes allow variable expansion while preventing word splitting and globbing of the result. Single quotes preserve literal characters. Pass untrusted values as arguments rather than building shell code and evaluating it.

lessons.title: Processes
lessons.summary: A process is a running program with credentials, memory mappings, file descriptors and scheduling state.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A process is a running program with credentials, memory mappings, file descriptors and scheduling state.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The kernel assigns a PID within a PID namespace. Child processes inherit selected state from their parent, and PIDs can be reused after exit. Check command, owner and start time before acting on a PID.

lessons.takeaway: The kernel assigns a PID within a PID namespace. Child processes inherit selected state from their parent, and PIDs can be reused after exit. Check command, owner and start time before acting on a PID.

lessons.title: Signals
lessons.summary: Signals notify a process of events such as termination requests or child exits.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Signals notify a process of events such as termination requests or child exits.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: SIGTERM can be handled for cleanup; SIGKILL cannot be caught. Graceful shutdown should stop new work, drain active work and exit within a deadline. A signal-based exit status alone does not establish why the signal was sent.

lessons.takeaway: SIGTERM can be handled for cleanup; SIGKILL cannot be caught. Graceful shutdown should stop new work, drain active work and exit within a deadline. A signal-based exit status alone does not establish why the signal was sent.

lessons.title: Disk blocks
lessons.summary: Filesystems allocate storage in blocks, and df reports allocation for a mounted filesystem.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Filesystems allocate storage in blocks, and df reports allocation for a mounted filesystem.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: du totals file usage visible through directory traversal. Open deleted files, snapshots, reserved space and mount boundaries can explain differences between the two. Inspect these causes before deleting data to chase a discrepancy.

lessons.takeaway: du totals file usage visible through directory traversal. Open deleted files, snapshots, reserved space and mount boundaries can explain differences between the two. Inspect these causes before deleting data to chase a discrepancy.

lessons.title: Inodes
lessons.summary: An inode stores file metadata and references to its data, separately from the filename in a directory.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: An inode stores file metadata and references to its data, separately from the filename in a directory.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Some filesystems have a bounded inode supply. Millions of tiny files can consume it while byte capacity remains. Check both block and inode utilization when creating files fails with no space left.

lessons.takeaway: Some filesystems have a bounded inode supply. Millions of tiny files can consume it while byte capacity remains. Check both block and inode utilization when creating files fails with no space left.

lessons.title: Open file limits
lessons.summary: A file descriptor is a process-local handle for an open file, socket, pipe or similar resource.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A file descriptor is a process-local handle for an open file, socket, pipe or similar resource.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The soft descriptor limit constrains normal allocation; the hard limit bounds unprivileged increases. Repeatedly rising descriptor counts may indicate a leak. Raising the limit without measuring demand can postpone rather than fix failure.

lessons.takeaway: The soft descriptor limit constrains normal allocation; the hard limit bounds unprivileged increases. Repeatedly rising descriptor counts may indicate a leak. Raising the limit without measuring demand can postpone rather than fix failure.

lessons.title: Load average
lessons.summary: Linux load average summarizes runnable tasks and tasks in uninterruptible sleep over time.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Linux load average summarizes runnable tasks and tasks in uninterruptible sleep over time.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The three values represent approximately one, five and fifteen minutes. Compare them with CPU count, task states and I/O latency. High load with idle CPU often requires investigating blocked I/O rather than adding cores.

lessons.takeaway: The three values represent approximately one, five and fifteen minutes. Compare them with CPU count, task states and I/O latency. High load with idle CPU often requires investigating blocked I/O rather than adding cores.

lessons.title: Memory cache
lessons.summary: The page cache keeps recently used file data in RAM to avoid repeated storage access.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: The page cache keeps recently used file data in RAM to avoid repeated storage access.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Much cached memory is reclaimable when applications need it. Available memory estimates usable headroom more meaningfully than free memory alone. Reclaim pressure, swap activity and latency distinguish useful caching from shortage.

lessons.takeaway: Much cached memory is reclaimable when applications need it. Available memory estimates usable headroom more meaningfully than free memory alone. Reclaim pressure, swap activity and latency distinguish useful caching from shortage.

lessons.title: OOM evidence
lessons.summary: An out-of-memory kill occurs when the kernel or a constrained memory cgroup cannot satisfy memory demand under its policy.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: An out-of-memory kill occurs when the kernel or a constrained memory cgroup cannot satisfy memory demand under its policy.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A cgroup can exhaust its own limit while the host has spare RAM. Confirm an OOM event through kernel logs or cgroup memory.events, then compare limits and workload growth. Exit 137 also occurs after other SIGKILL events.

lessons.takeaway: A cgroup can exhaust its own limit while the host has spare RAM. Confirm an OOM event through kernel logs or cgroup memory.events, then compare limits and workload growth. Exit 137 also occurs after other SIGKILL events.

lessons.title: Socket inspection
lessons.summary: A socket is an endpoint for network or local interprocess communication.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A socket is an endpoint for network or local interprocess communication.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Listening sockets accept new connections; established sockets carry active conversations. A listener bound to 127.0.0.1 is not exposed on the host's external interface. Inspect protocol, address and port before changing network rules.

lessons.takeaway: Listening sockets accept new connections; established sockets carry active conversations. A listener bound to 127.0.0.1 is not exposed on the host's external interface. Inspect protocol, address and port before changing network rules.

lessons.title: Name resolution
lessons.summary: Linux name-service resolution maps names to records using configured sources such as local files and DNS.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Linux name-service resolution maps names to records using configured sources such as local files and DNS.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: NSS configuration controls lookup order for applications using the system resolver. A direct DNS query does not test local hosts entries or every application's private cache. Compare getent results with DNS responses and application behavior.

lessons.takeaway: NSS configuration controls lookup order for applications using the system resolver. A direct DNS query does not test local hosts entries or every application's private cache. Compare getent results with DNS responses and application behavior.

lessons.title: Mount options
lessons.summary: A mount attaches a filesystem view to a directory and applies options to that view.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A mount attaches a filesystem view to a directory and applies options to that view.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Read-only, noexec, nosuid and nodev constrain different operations. File mode bits cannot override a read-only mount. A filesystem unexpectedly remounted read-only may signal storage errors that require investigation before restoring writes.

lessons.takeaway: Read-only, noexec, nosuid and nodev constrain different operations. File mode bits cannot override a read-only mount. A filesystem unexpectedly remounted read-only may signal storage errors that require investigation before restoring writes.

lessons.title: Deleted executables
lessons.summary: A process can retain mappings to executable data after its pathname has been removed or replaced.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A process can retain mappings to executable data after its pathname has been removed or replaced.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Replacing a package on disk does not switch an existing process to the new code. Controlled restarts are often needed after updates. Inspect mapped executable versions and service start times when verifying patch completion.

lessons.takeaway: Replacing a package on disk does not switch an existing process to the new code. Controlled restarts are often needed after updates. Inspect mapped executable versions and service start times when verifying patch completion.

lessons.title: Zombies
lessons.summary: A zombie is an exited child process whose parent has not yet collected its exit status.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A zombie is an exited child process whose parent has not yet collected its exit status.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: It no longer runs application code but retains a process-table entry. The parent should call a wait operation or otherwise arrange child reaping. Killing the zombie again is ineffective; investigate the parent's lifecycle handling.

lessons.takeaway: It no longer runs application code but retains a process-table entry. The parent should call a wait operation or otherwise arrange child reaping. Killing the zombie again is ineffective; investigate the parent's lifecycle handling.

lessons.title: System calls
lessons.summary: A system call is a controlled request from user space to the kernel for services such as file I/O or memory mapping.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A system call is a controlled request from user space to the kernel for services such as file I/O or memory mapping.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Tracing shows call arguments, return codes and timing, making permission failures and blocking operations visible. It can add overhead and reveal sensitive arguments, so trace a narrow process and time window.

lessons.takeaway: Tracing shows call arguments, return codes and timing, making permission failures and blocking operations visible. It can add overhead and reveal sensitive arguments, so trace a narrow process and time window.

lessons.title: Scheduling priority
lessons.summary: The normal Linux scheduler shares CPU among runnable tasks using scheduling weights and other controls.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: The normal Linux scheduler shares CPU among runnable tasks using scheduling weights and other controls.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Nice values influence relative weight; a larger nice value usually means less preference. They do not impose a hard CPU ceiling or guarantee latency. Cgroup bandwidth limits and placement solve different problems.

lessons.takeaway: Nice values influence relative weight; a larger nice value usually means less preference. They do not impose a hard CPU ceiling or guarantee latency. Cgroup bandwidth limits and placement solve different problems.

lessons.title: Swap pressure
lessons.summary: Swap provides backing storage for selected memory pages when the kernel moves them out of RAM.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Swap provides backing storage for selected memory pages when the kernel moves them out of RAM.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Configured swap is not itself a fault. Sustained swap-in and swap-out combined with reclaim stalls and latency suggests working-set pressure. Disabling swap under pressure can instead force allocation failures or OOM kills.

lessons.takeaway: Configured swap is not itself a fault. Sustained swap-in and swap-out combined with reclaim stalls and latency suggests working-set pressure. Disabling swap under pressure can instead force allocation failures or OOM kills.

lessons.title: Capabilities
lessons.summary: Linux capabilities divide traditional root privileges into more specific permissions.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Linux capabilities divide traditional root privileges into more specific permissions.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A process may receive narrowly scoped powers such as binding privileged ports. Effective, permitted and other capability sets determine what can be exercised or inherited. Some capabilities remain very powerful, so combine them with other isolation controls.

lessons.takeaway: A process may receive narrowly scoped powers such as binding privileged ports. Effective, permitted and other capability sets determine what can be exercised or inherited. Some capabilities remain very powerful, so combine them with other isolation controls.

lessons.title: ACL masks
lessons.summary: POSIX ACLs extend the owner/group/other model with named users and groups.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: POSIX ACLs extend the owner/group/other model with named users and groups.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The ACL mask caps the effective rights of named users and the group class. An entry may display write permission while its effective rights exclude write. Default directory ACLs influence new entries but do not retroactively update existing files.

lessons.takeaway: The ACL mask caps the effective rights of named users and the group class. An entry may display write permission while its effective rights exclude write. Default directory ACLs influence new entries but do not retroactively update existing files.

lessons.title: Atomic replacement
lessons.summary: Atomic replacement publishes a complete new file by renaming it over the old directory entry on the same filesystem.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Atomic replacement publishes a complete new file by renaming it over the old directory entry on the same filesystem.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Readers opening the path see an old or new version rather than a partly written file. Existing open descriptors may still read the old inode. Crash durability additionally needs appropriate file and directory synchronization; atomic visibility alone is insufficient.

lessons.takeaway: Readers opening the path see an old or new version rather than a partly written file. Existing open descriptors may still read the old inode. Crash durability additionally needs appropriate file and directory synchronization; atomic visibility alone is insufficient.

lessons.title: Namespaces
lessons.summary: Namespaces give processes separate views of resources such as PIDs, mounts, networks and hostnames.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Namespaces give processes separate views of resources such as PIDs, mounts, networks and hostnames.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: They control visibility and identity boundaries. Two processes in different network namespaces can have separate routing tables while still sharing CPU and the kernel. Cgroups provide resource accounting and limits rather than namespace visibility.

lessons.takeaway: They control visibility and identity boundaries. Two processes in different network namespaces can have separate routing tables while still sharing CPU and the kernel. Cgroups provide resource accounting and limits rather than namespace visibility.

lessons.title: Cgroup throttling
lessons.summary: Control groups account for and constrain resource use by groups of processes.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Control groups account for and constrain resource use by groups of processes.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A CPU quota limits runnable time during a scheduling period. A group can be throttled even when other host cores are idle. Compare throttling counters, quotas and latency before raising a limit or changing concurrency.

lessons.takeaway: A CPU quota limits runnable time during a scheduling period. A group can be throttled even when other host cores are idle. Compare throttling counters, quotas and latency before raising a limit or changing concurrency.

lessons.title: Filesystem recovery
lessons.summary: Filesystem recovery restores metadata consistency after damage or an unclean failure.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Filesystem recovery restores metadata consistency after damage or an unclean failure.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Tools and procedures depend on the filesystem. Stop uncontrolled writes, preserve recoverable data and use the supported offline or online process. Repairing an actively writable filesystem with an offline repair tool can worsen corruption.

lessons.takeaway: Tools and procedures depend on the filesystem. Stop uncontrolled writes, preserve recoverable data and use the supported offline or online process. Repairing an actively writable filesystem with an offline repair tool can worsen corruption.

lessons.title: Clock selection
lessons.summary: Wall clocks represent calendar time; monotonic clocks measure elapsed time within a system's clock domain.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Wall clocks represent calendar time; monotonic clocks measure elapsed time within a system's clock domain.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Clock synchronization or administrative changes can adjust wall time. Deadlines and durations should use an appropriate monotonic source, while distributed logs need synchronized wall timestamps and correlation IDs. Monotonic timestamps from different hosts are not directly comparable.

lessons.takeaway: Clock synchronization or administrative changes can adjust wall time. Deadlines and durations should use an appropriate monotonic source, while distributed logs need synchronized wall timestamps and correlation IDs. Monotonic timestamps from different hosts are not directly comparable.

lessons.title: Kernel versus user space
lessons.summary: User space runs ordinary applications; the kernel mediates privileged access to hardware and shared resources.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: User space runs ordinary applications; the kernel mediates privileged access to hardware and shared resources.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Applications request kernel services through system calls. Device, filesystem and kernel failures can affect unrelated applications simultaneously. Shared symptoms and kernel logs help distinguish infrastructure faults from a single application's logic.

lessons.takeaway: Applications request kernel services through system calls. Device, filesystem and kernel failures can affect unrelated applications simultaneously. Shared symptoms and kernel logs help distinguish infrastructure faults from a single application's logic.

commands.title: Inspect identity
commands.definition: Prints the current user's UID, primary group and supplementary groups.
commands.purpose: Check the credentials involved in a permission failure.
commands.environment: Read-only; run in the same identity context as the failing process.
commands.interpretation: uid is the user identity; gid is the primary group; groups lists additional memberships.
commands.safety: Read-only; run in the same identity context as the failing process.

commands.title: Inspect path permissions
commands.definition: Walks a path and displays permissions and ownership for each component.
commands.purpose: Locate a parent directory that blocks traversal despite readable file permissions.
commands.environment: Read-only; replace the example path. namei is commonly supplied by util-linux.
commands.interpretation: Each row is a path component; directory execute permission is required for traversal.
commands.safety: Read-only; replace the example path. namei is commonly supplied by util-linux.

commands.title: Disk capacity
commands.definition: Reports mounted-filesystem block capacity with readable units and filesystem type.
commands.purpose: Identify the full filesystem before cleaning or expanding storage.
commands.environment: Read-only; compare the mount containing the failing path.
commands.expectedOutput: Filesystem Type Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on
commands.interpretation: Use% is block utilization; Mounted on identifies the mount, not just a directory name.
commands.safety: Read-only; compare the mount containing the failing path.

commands.title: Inode capacity
commands.definition: Reports inode allocation for mounted filesystems.
commands.purpose: Detect no-space failures caused by many small files.
commands.environment: Read-only; inode semantics vary by filesystem.
commands.expectedOutput: Filesystem Inodes IUsed IFree IUse% Mounted on
commands.interpretation: IUse% tracks inode use; free bytes can remain when IFree reaches zero.
commands.safety: Read-only; inode semantics vary by filesystem.

commands.title: Memory headroom
commands.definition: Summarizes memory and swap accounting.
commands.purpose: Distinguish reclaimable cache from genuine memory shortage.
commands.environment: Read-only; correlate with pressure and swap activity.
commands.expectedOutput: Mem: total used free shared buff/cache available
commands.interpretation: Available is estimated usable headroom; free alone excludes useful reclaimable cache.
commands.safety: Read-only; correlate with pressure and swap activity.

commands.title: Process states
commands.definition: Prints selected fields for every visible process.
commands.purpose: Find parent-child relationships, zombies and blocked tasks.
commands.environment: Read-only; visibility depends on namespace and permissions.
commands.expectedOutput: PID PPID USER STAT ELAPSED COMMAND
commands.interpretation: STAT includes R for runnable, S for interruptible sleep, D for uninterruptible sleep and Z for zombie; ETIME is elapsed lifetime.
commands.safety: Read-only; visibility depends on namespace and permissions.

commands.title: Listening sockets
commands.definition: Lists listening TCP sockets numerically and requests process information.
commands.purpose: Check whether a service listens on the expected address and port.
commands.environment: Read-only; loopback binding is not external reachability.
commands.interpretation: -l selects listeners, -n avoids name lookup, -t selects TCP, -p adds process data when permitted.
commands.safety: Read-only; loopback binding is not external reachability.

commands.title: System activity
commands.definition: Samples process, memory, paging, I/O and CPU counters five times.
commands.purpose: Separate CPU contention, swapping and I/O waits.
commands.environment: Read-only; interpret several signals together rather than one column.
commands.expectedOutput: r b swpd free buff cache si so bi bo in cs us sy id wa st
commands.interpretation: The first row summarizes since boot; later rows cover intervals. r is runnable tasks, b is blocked tasks, si/so are swap traffic.
commands.safety: Read-only; interpret several signals together rather than one column.

commands.title: Kernel events
commands.definition: Shows recent kernel journal messages.
commands.purpose: Find OOM, device and filesystem evidence near an incident.
commands.environment: Read-only; access and retention vary, and logs may contain sensitive metadata.
commands.interpretation: -k selects kernel messages; --since bounds time. Match timestamps and affected devices or cgroups.
commands.safety: Read-only; access and retention vary, and logs may contain sensitive metadata.

commands.title: Mount inspection
commands.definition: Displays mounted filesystems and selected fields.
commands.purpose: Find read-only mounts or unexpected backing devices.
commands.environment: Read-only; do not remount until the reason for read-only state is understood.
commands.interpretation: TARGET is the path; SOURCE is the backing object; ro in OPTIONS means read-only.
commands.safety: Read-only; do not remount until the reason for read-only state is understood.

commands.title: Open deleted files
commands.definition: Lists open files with link counts below one.
commands.purpose: Explain disk space retained after a log was deleted.
commands.environment: Read-only but may require elevated visibility; do not kill a process solely from this output.
commands.interpretation: Look at COMMAND, PID, SIZE/OFF and NAME marked deleted; the process still holds the inode.
commands.safety: Read-only but may require elevated visibility; do not kill a process solely from this output.

commands.title: System resolver
commands.definition: Queries the configured name-service lookup path.
commands.purpose: Compare application-style resolution with direct DNS tools.
commands.environment: Read-only; example addresses are illustrative and actual results differ.
commands.interpretation: Returned addresses follow system NSS behavior and can include local overrides.
commands.safety: Read-only; example addresses are illustrative and actual results differ.

commands.title: List metadata
commands.definition: Lists directory entries with mode, owner, size and modification time.
commands.purpose: Compare visible file attributes during access or deployment checks.
commands.environment: Read-only; listing a directory requires access to it and does not prove every file is readable.
commands.interpretation: The first character is file type; the next nine are permission bits. -a includes dotfiles; sizes are readable units.
commands.safety: Read-only; listing a directory requires access to it and does not prove every file is readable.

commands.title: Precise file metadata
commands.definition: Reports inode metadata and timestamps for a filesystem object.
commands.purpose: Check ownership, permissions, link count and actual allocated storage.
commands.environment: Read-only; use the intended path and distinguish metadata change from content modification.
commands.interpretation: Size is logical length; Blocks reports allocated blocks. Access, Modify and Change are different timestamps.
commands.safety: Read-only; use the intended path and distinguish metadata change from content modification.

commands.title: Directory usage
commands.definition: Totals allocated space beneath a directory one level deep.
commands.purpose: Find which directory contributes to a full filesystem.
commands.environment: Read-only but can generate substantial I/O; permissions can prevent a complete scan. GNU du syntax.
commands.interpretation: -x stays on one filesystem; -d1 limits display depth. Totals can differ from df for open deleted files and filesystem metadata.
commands.safety: Read-only but can generate substantial I/O; permissions can prevent a complete scan. GNU du syntax.

commands.title: Find old files
commands.definition: Finds regular files whose modification age exceeds the specified day boundary.
commands.purpose: Inventory retention candidates before deciding what to remove.
commands.environment: Read-only example; inspect results and retention requirements before adding any deleting action.
commands.interpretation: -xdev avoids other mounted filesystems; -mtime counts rounded 24-hour periods. Output is matching paths, not deletion confirmation.
commands.safety: Read-only example; inspect results and retention requirements before adding any deleting action.

commands.title: Search log context
commands.definition: Finds matching lines and nearby context in a text file.
commands.purpose: Locate an error with enough surrounding information to interpret it.
commands.environment: Read-only; logs may contain sensitive fields. A missing match can mean wrong time window or file.
commands.interpretation: -n prints line numbers; -C 2 adds two lines on each side. -- ends option parsing.
commands.safety: Read-only; logs may contain sensitive fields. A missing match can mean wrong time window or file.

commands.title: Follow rotating logs
commands.definition: Displays the end of a file and follows its name across replacement.
commands.purpose: Observe new messages from an application that rotates log files.
commands.environment: Read-only; stop with Ctrl-C and protect sensitive log output.
commands.interpretation: -F follows by name and retries if the path disappears; new lines are live output, not a complete incident history.
commands.safety: Read-only; stop with Ctrl-C and protect sensitive log output.

commands.title: Bounded file inspection
commands.definition: Prints the first twenty lines of a file.
commands.purpose: Inspect a file format without dumping the entire file to the terminal.
commands.environment: Read-only; do not use indiscriminately on secret files.
commands.interpretation: -n sets the line count; output preserves the selected lines, including comments.
commands.safety: Read-only; do not use indiscriminately on secret files.

commands.title: Interactive file reading
commands.definition: Opens a pager for navigating text without editing it.
commands.purpose: Read a large log and search for a known incident marker.
commands.environment: Read-only viewing; the pager may offer shell features, so it is not a security sandbox.
commands.interpretation: Use /pattern to search, n for the next match and q to quit; position is within the opened file.
commands.safety: Read-only viewing; the pager may offer shell features, so it is not a security sandbox.

commands.title: ACL inspection
commands.definition: Displays POSIX access-control entries and their effective permissions.
commands.purpose: Diagnose access that cannot be explained by mode bits alone.
commands.environment: Read-only; ACL tooling and filesystem support must be installed.
commands.interpretation: Named-user and group-class entries can be limited by mask; an effective comment shows the resulting rights.
commands.safety: Read-only; ACL tooling and filesystem support must be installed.

commands.title: Scoped permission change
commands.definition: Sets explicit owner, group and other permission bits on one file.
commands.purpose: Apply a reviewed file-access policy without recursive broad changes.
commands.environment: Mutates file permissions; verify file identity, intended owner/group and parent traversal first.
commands.expectedOutput: No output on success; stat shows 640
commands.interpretation: No output normally means success; inspect with stat afterward. This example sets mode 640.
commands.safety: Mutates file permissions; verify file identity, intended owner/group and parent traversal first.

commands.title: Scoped ownership change
commands.definition: Changes the owner and group of a selected filesystem object.
commands.purpose: Align a file with an approved service identity and access group.
commands.environment: Requires authority to change ownership; affects access and can clear special mode bits. Avoid recursive use without review.
commands.interpretation: app is the owner and readers is the group; success is normally silent. Verify with stat or ls.
commands.safety: Requires authority to change ownership; affects access and can clear special mode bits. Avoid recursive use without review.

commands.title: Resolve a link
commands.definition: Resolves links and prints a canonicalized path.
commands.purpose: Find the release directory selected by a deployment link.
commands.environment: Read-only; -f behavior is GNU/coreutils-style and does not prove the application has reloaded the target.
commands.interpretation: The output is the resolved path, not the contents of the target; missing path components can cause failure.
commands.safety: Read-only; -f behavior is GNU/coreutils-style and does not prove the application has reloaded the target.

commands.title: Process lookup
commands.definition: Lists processes whose full command line matches an expression.
commands.purpose: Find candidate processes before inspecting identity or sending signals.
commands.environment: Read-only; verify the result and process start time. Arguments may contain sensitive data.
commands.interpretation: Each row begins with a PID followed by its command line; a substring can match unrelated processes.
commands.safety: Read-only; verify the result and process start time. Arguments may contain sensitive data.

commands.title: Graceful termination
commands.definition: Sends a termination request to one process.
commands.purpose: Allow a process to perform its supported shutdown handling.
commands.environment: Changes process state; confirm identity, ownership and service-manager restart policy before use.
commands.expectedOutput: No output on successful signal delivery
commands.interpretation: Replace PID with a verified current process ID. A successful send does not prove cleanup or exit has completed.
commands.safety: Changes process state; confirm identity, ownership and service-manager restart policy before use.

commands.title: Live process view
commands.definition: Shows repeated resource and state information for a selected process.
commands.purpose: Observe whether demand or state changes while reproducing a problem.
commands.environment: Read-only inspection; some interactive keys can change priorities or send signals, so use deliberately.
commands.expectedOutput: PID USER PR NI VIRT RES SHR S %CPU %MEM TIME+ COMMAND
commands.interpretation: %CPU describes CPU use over sampling intervals; RES is resident memory. Press q to exit.
commands.safety: Read-only inspection; some interactive keys can change priorities or send signals, so use deliberately.

commands.title: Per-process activity
commands.definition: Samples CPU-related activity for one process five times.
commands.purpose: Correlate a specific process with an incident instead of relying on host averages.
commands.environment: Read-only; requires sysstat. Replace PID and compare with workload timing.
commands.interpretation: Each interval reports the selected PID; %CPU and CPU indicate use and execution CPU. PID may exit during sampling.
commands.safety: Read-only; requires sysstat. Replace PID and compare with workload timing.

commands.title: Storage latency
commands.definition: Reports extended device I/O statistics at one-second intervals.
commands.purpose: Investigate storage delay and queueing during a slowdown.
commands.environment: Read-only; requires sysstat. The first report covers since boot unless configured otherwise.
commands.expectedOutput: Device r/s w/s r_await w_await aqu-sz %util
commands.interpretation: await is average I/O completion time; aqu-sz is average queue length. %util alone is not a universal saturation limit for parallel devices.
commands.safety: Read-only; requires sysstat. The first report covers since boot unless configured otherwise.

commands.title: Pressure stalls
commands.definition: Reads Linux pressure-stall information for memory.
commands.purpose: Check whether memory contention is delaying runnable work.
commands.environment: Read-only; requires a kernel exposing PSI. Host and cgroup scope are different.
commands.interpretation: some measures intervals with at least one task stalled; full measures all non-idle tasks stalled. avg10/60/300 are percentage windows.
commands.safety: Read-only; requires a kernel exposing PSI. Host and cgroup scope are different.

commands.title: Process descriptor limits
commands.definition: Displays the running process's resource limits.
commands.purpose: Check the effective open-file limit rather than assuming the interactive shell's limit applies.
commands.environment: Read-only; replace PID. Visibility depends on procfs permissions and process lifetime.
commands.interpretation: Max open files has soft and hard limits; the soft limit is the active boundary for normal allocation.
commands.safety: Read-only; replace PID. Visibility depends on procfs permissions and process lifetime.

commands.title: Process file descriptors
commands.definition: Lists a process's open descriptor links.
commands.purpose: Inspect whether sockets, files or pipes dominate descriptor usage.
commands.environment: Read-only; access may be restricted. The process can open or close descriptors while you inspect it.
commands.interpretation: Each filename is a descriptor number; the link target identifies the opened object, sometimes marked deleted.
commands.safety: Read-only; access may be restricted. The process can open or close descriptors while you inspect it.

commands.title: Trace selected calls
commands.definition: Attaches a syscall tracer and follows child processes for file-related calls.
commands.purpose: Find pathname failures such as ENOENT or EACCES when logs are insufficient.
commands.environment: Diagnostic attachment can slow the target and reveal paths; obtain incident authority and keep the capture brief.
commands.interpretation: A call's return value and errno show the kernel result; unfinished calls may be blocked rather than failed.
commands.safety: Diagnostic attachment can slow the target and reveal paths; obtain incident authority and keep the capture brief.

commands.title: User and group lookup
commands.definition: Queries the system account database for an account.
commands.purpose: Check the UID, primary GID, home and shell associated with a service name.
commands.environment: Read-only; results may come from local files or a configured directory service.
commands.interpretation: Colon-separated fields include name, password placeholder, UID, GID, description, home and shell.
commands.safety: Read-only; results may come from local files or a configured directory service.

references.title: User and group lookup — primary documentation

commands.title: File capabilities
commands.definition: Displays file-based Linux capabilities attached to an executable.
commands.purpose: Review privileges granted outside normal owner/group mode bits.
commands.environment: Read-only; requires capability tools. Review the complete privilege model, not this one output alone.
commands.interpretation: The capability list and flags describe enabled file capabilities; empty output can mean none are set.
commands.safety: Read-only; requires capability tools. Review the complete privilege model, not this one output alone.

commands.title: Archive inventory
commands.definition: Lists members of an archive without extracting them.
commands.purpose: Inspect backup contents and path names before a restore.
commands.environment: Read-only; review paths and trusted origin before extraction, especially with elevated privileges.
commands.interpretation: -t lists and -f selects the archive file. Output shows member names, not a verified successful application restore.
commands.safety: Read-only; review paths and trusted origin before extraction, especially with elevated privileges.

commands.title: Checksum verification
commands.definition: Computes a SHA-256 digest of a file.
commands.purpose: Compare an artifact with an independently trusted expected digest.
commands.environment: Read-only; obtain the expected checksum from an authenticated source.
commands.interpretation: The first field is the hex digest and the second is the filename; equal digests support byte identity, not publisher trust by themselves.
commands.safety: Read-only; obtain the expected checksum from an authenticated source.

commands.title: Structured JSON inspection
commands.definition: Selects a field from a JSON document.
commands.purpose: Read a structured API result without unreliable text slicing.
commands.environment: Read-only; jq must be installed. Avoid printing credential fields into shared logs.
commands.interpretation: Objects and arrays remain structured; null can mean the selected field is absent. Invalid JSON causes an error.
commands.safety: Read-only; jq must be installed. Avoid printing credential fields into shared logs.

commands.title: Line and byte counts
commands.definition: Counts newline characters and bytes in a file.
commands.purpose: Measure a text file's size and line growth during investigation.
commands.environment: Read-only; reading a large active file adds I/O and is only a point-in-time observation.
commands.interpretation: The first numeric column is line count and the second is bytes; a final unterminated line affects interpretation.
commands.safety: Read-only; reading a large active file adds I/O and is only a point-in-time observation.

references.title: Line and byte counts — primary documentation

commands.title: Command discovery
commands.definition: Reports how the current shell resolves a command name.
commands.purpose: Compare interactive and scheduled-job PATH behavior.
commands.environment: Read-only shell builtin; run in the same environment as the failing job.
commands.interpretation: A path identifies the executable found; no output with failure status means no matching command was resolved.
commands.safety: Read-only shell builtin; run in the same environment as the failing job.

debugging.title: Readable file still denied
debugging.symptom: The service belongs to the file's group but cannot open a mode-640 configuration.

steps.evidence: Compare the service UID/groups with each path component. A parent directory without search permission blocks access before the file's read bit matters. Also inspect ACL effective rights when present.
Grant the intended identity narrowly scoped traversal and file access; preserve restrictions for other users. Do not apply recursive 777.
Open the file as the actual service identity and confirm unrelated identities remain denied.

references.title: Readable file still denied — primary documentation

debugging.title: Disk full after deleting logs
debugging.symptom: df reports nearly full storage while du shows much less visible data.

steps.evidence: Find large deleted files still open by a process and confirm their device matches the full mount. Also account for snapshots and mount boundaries.
Use the application's supported log reopen or a controlled restart after assessing impact. Correct rotation so future logs reopen properly.
Confirm free blocks recover and new logs continue arriving at the expected path.

references.title: Disk full after deleting logs — primary documentation

debugging.title: No space with free gigabytes
debugging.symptom: Creating files fails even though byte capacity remains.

steps.evidence: Check IFree and IUse% on the affected mount. Identify a directory generating excessive small files before deleting anything.
Remove only confirmed disposable files under a retention policy and fix the producer or lifecycle rule. Plan filesystem capacity if the workload is legitimate.
Confirm inode headroom and successful file creation; observe growth over the next workload cycle.

references.title: No space with free gigabytes — primary documentation

debugging.title: High load and idle CPU
debugging.symptom: Requests slow down while load average rises but CPU remains mostly idle.

steps.evidence: Inspect blocked tasks, I/O waits and storage latency. Correlate D-state processes with a device or network filesystem; load alone does not identify the bottleneck.
Reduce or pause the offending I/O workload, restore the storage path, or shift traffic using a tested procedure. Avoid treating CPU expansion as the first fix.
Verify blocked-task count, storage latency and application response times recover together.

references.title: High load and idle CPU — primary documentation

debugging.title: Too many open files
debugging.symptom: A service rejects connections with descriptor-allocation errors.

steps.evidence: Compare the actual process limit with descriptor counts and types over time. A steadily rising count under stable traffic suggests a leak; a bounded peak may be legitimate demand.
Fix leaked handles or unbounded connection creation. If demand is valid, raise the service limit within host capacity and roll out safely.
Repeat the workload and verify descriptor counts stabilize below the limit without increased host pressure.

references.title: Too many open files — primary documentation

debugging.title: Exit 137 after deployment
debugging.symptom: A containerized process disappears with exit status 137.

steps.evidence: Look for a matching OOM event and inspect the relevant cgroup memory.events and limit. Also check operator or orchestrator termination; the exit code alone only suggests SIGKILL.
If memory pressure is confirmed, roll back a regression or adjust measured capacity and concurrency. If another actor killed it, correct that lifecycle behavior.
Verify the termination reason no longer recurs and memory/latency remain stable at representative load.

debugging.title: Local service unreachable remotely
debugging.symptom: curl on localhost succeeds but clients on another host fail.

steps.evidence: Check whether the listener binds only to 127.0.0.1 and confirm the intended port. If it listens externally, inspect routing and firewall evidence next.
Bind to the intended interface and apply only the required network access rules. Do not disable the firewall globally.
Test from an authorized remote client and verify unauthorized networks remain blocked.

references.title: Local service unreachable remotely — primary documentation

debugging.title: Read-only filesystem
debugging.symptom: Writes fail with read-only filesystem after device warnings.

steps.evidence: Confirm the mount is ro and correlate kernel messages with the backing device. Distinguish an intentional read-only mount from protective remount after errors.
Protect recoverable data, stop affected writers and follow filesystem-specific recovery. Do not force a writable remount while underlying corruption remains unresolved.
Validate filesystem health and restored writes through an application-level check before returning full traffic.

debugging.title: Zombie accumulation
debugging.symptom: A service accumulates many Z-state child processes.

steps.evidence: Group zombies by parent PID and check whether the parent collects child exit status. The children have already exited and cannot be repaired by another kill signal.
Correct the parent's wait/reaping behavior; use a controlled parent restart as mitigation if appropriate. Container init behavior may need correction.
Run repeated child workloads and confirm process-table entries are reaped rather than accumulating.

debugging.title: Latency under CPU quota
debugging.symptom: A service's latency rises even though host cores are idle.

steps.evidence: Read the affected cgroup's throttling counters over time, not necessarily the root cgroup. Compare quota, concurrency and latency in the same interval.
Tune quota or workload concurrency based on demand and host capacity. Preserve isolation requirements rather than removing all limits.
Verify throttling and tail latency improve under representative traffic without starving neighbors.

references.title: Latency under CPU quota — primary documentation
